Houthi attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha killed three people and wounded 36, Saudi Arabia said; the Saudi-led coalition then struck 82 Houthi targets. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Abha International Airport and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were attacked on Oct. 6 and 7; an Egyptian and an Algerian were killed at Abha and a Sudanese national in Riyadh. The Houthis said they fired a ballistic missile at the Riyadh airport, their second claimed attack on it this week; the coalition said that missile was intercepted. The coalition said it then destroyed 82 military targets, including mountain missile sites and command centers, AFP reported.

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration over $20 million in taxpayer-funded TV ads it calls illegal pro-Trump propaganda. The complaint, filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Washington, names President Trump, the White House, Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, and asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop federal money from paying for them. The ads, marked 'Paid for by the U.S. Government,' began airing in September; $20 million has been drawn from a $175 million DHS immigration-enforcement fund, and more than $12 million had been spent so far, AP reported, citing AdImpact. No ruling yet.

Texas executed Jamaal Howard, the first U.S. execution since Tennessee's failed lethal injection of Christa Pike a week earlier. Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. CT Wednesday in Huntsville after a dose of pentobarbital, the same drug used on Pike. He was convicted of killing store clerk Vickie Swartout in a 2000 robbery. The Supreme Court denied his requests to stop the execution; only Justice Jackson said she would grant a stay. AP said it was the 30th U.S. execution this year.

NHC director Michael Brennan said it could reach Category 3 before landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Florida declared a state of emergency for more than a third of its counties, and producers shut in a significant share of Gulf offshore oil and gas output, AP reported.

A Russian cruise missile hit a residential building in Pryluky, Chernihiv region, killing 19 people, five of them children, and injuring 55, Ukraine's emergency service said as rescuers kept searching the rubble. Authorities count at least 30 dead and 138 injured across Ukraine over the past day, including three in Kyiv and two each in Kremenchuk, Kirovohrad and Sumy regions. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired ballistic missiles, 48 cruise missiles (39 stopped) and 130 drones (117 stopped).

Separately, Russian officials said they intercepted almost 900 Ukrainian drones overnight.

The tanker Acers was hit by multiple projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Qatar, with casualties, Britain's UKMTO said. UKMTO said the master reported the strike at about 3 p.m. ET Wednesday, about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar; it gave no casualty count. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the ship as the Antigua-flagged, Greek-managed tanker Acers. It is the first reported tanker attack in the western Gulf in weeks, far from the Strait of Hormuz.

Wells Fargo's programs to raise Black homeownership are under a Fair Housing Act investigation by HUD. HUD Secretary Scott Turner announced the probe Oct. 7, and HUD sent a letter to Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf saying it will examine whether the bank offered different products or terms based on race. The programs date to the bank's 2017 pledge of $60 billion in loans to add 250,000 Black homeowners by 2027, expanded in 2022 to refinancing for minority homeowners. Findings could lead to charges or a Justice Department referral; this is an investigation, not a finding.

An 18-year-old was charged with planning a terror attack on the Mall of America after buying an AK-47 from undercover FBI agents, prosecutors say. Federal prosecutors in Minnesota say Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a U.S.-born citizen, was arrested Tuesday in a Richfield park after paying $600 for an AK-47 and 200 rounds to an undercover FBI employee posing as an ISIS member. The complaint alleges he told an informant he planned to kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24. U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said he spoke of killing 30 to 60 people. Social Security identity-theft victims will get a single point of contact at the agency under a law President Trump signed Wednesday. H.R. 5345, the Improving Social Security's Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act, requires the Social Security Administration to give one point of contact to people whose number has been misused or whose card was lost. Trump also signed S. 766, the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, which requires a yearly report on federally funded projects more than five years behind schedule or more than $1 billion over budget.

Saudi Arabia launched an air-safety investigation into the Flydubai FZ1073 cockpit attack, separate from the UAE's criminal probe, Reuters reported. Three people close to the matter told Reuters on Wednesday that Saudi Arabia notified aviation agencies abroad it will run a safety investigation under international rules, because the flight was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board confirmed it assigned a representative, since the Boeing 737 MAX was built in the United States. Optional Practical Training for foreign students would cost $70,000 per student under a Homeland Security proposal filed Wednesday. The ICE proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student's first OPT period and $30,000 for each later one; schools would recommend OPT only for students whose fee they pay. DHS says that without the fees it may shut the program down entirely. Comments are due 30 days after publication. It is a proposal, not a final rule.

Imports worth $2,500 or less would face tighter filing and bond rules under a Customs and Border Protection proposal filed Wednesday. The CBP proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would change filing rules for informal entries of $2,500 or less, create a new electronic entry type for mailed packages, require mail carriers to send an extra data element, and require a basic import bond for some informal entries. Comments are due 60 days after publication.

Yemen's Houthis fired ballistic missiles and drones at Aden's international airport, forcing a Cairo flight to divert, as Saudi Arabia downed a missile near Riyadh. Drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire inside Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, Bulgaria said; the sunken ship's crew is missing. Sea and air drones hit the two ships about 70 nautical miles east of Byala early Tuesday local time. The Togo-flagged, Turkish-owned Alfa Watan sank and its crew is unaccounted for. The Palau-flagged Able, carrying wheat, caught fire; all 18 crew were rescued and taken to Varna, and one is in critical condition with severe burns. Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack "absolutely unacceptable" and said the drones were "clearly either Russian or Ukrainian"; who launched them has not been established. Ukraine launched about 650 drones at Moscow overnight, killing two people in one of the largest attacks on the Russian capital in two years, Russian officials said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said most of the drones were shot down, 105 of them close to the city. Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said one person died in Radumlya and one in Barybino, and a drone set a retail warehouse on fire in Litvinovo. Reports put the injured at six to nine. The 650 figure comes from Russian officials; Ukraine has not confirmed it. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck Ukraine's Black Sea ports of Chornomorsk and Izmail overnight.

The S&P 500 closed at a record high Tuesday, its first since August, as Treasury yields eased from their highest levels since 2002. The S&P 500 rose 44.98 points, or 0.6%, to 7,818.93. The Dow gained 253.38 to 51,521.28, and the Nasdaq rose 122.48 to 27,599.79, its second straight record. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.28% from 5.31% late Monday. The S&P 500 is up 23% from its late-March low.

Anduril and the Navy will spend $6.6 billion on a new Baltimore County shipyard to build Virginia-class submarine parts, the White House announced. Anduril is investing $3.7 billion and the Navy committed up to $2.9 billion through a contract for the facility, called Arsenal-2, at Tradepoint Atlantic. Maryland officials said it will create more than 3,100 permanent jobs; initial operations are targeted for 2030. President Trump promoted the project Tuesday.

A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration's policy of fining migrants up to $1.8 million for not leaving the U.S. after final deportation orders. U.S. District Judge George O'Toole stayed the ICE rule used to impose the fines and barred enforcement of fines issued after June 27, 2025, while a class-action lawsuit brought by two fined migrants moves forward, Reuters reported Monday. He found the fines were likely imposed unlawfully, including because ICE skipped public notice and comment and the Department of Homeland Security did not consider individual circumstances. Since last year the administration has levied fines of $998 a day, applied retroactively for up to five years. DHS said in July it had issued more than 100,000 such fines totaling about $84 billion.

Twelve sailors were injured when a projectile hit the tanker On Peace in the Strait of Hormuz, India's foreign ministry said. World oil production will fall about 5 million barrels a day this year because of the Iran war, the Energy Information Administration projected. In its Oct. 6 Short-Term Energy Outlook, EIA projected world petroleum production falling from a record 106.3 million barrels a day in 2025 to 101.1 million in 2026, and world demand falling from 104.4 million to 102.4 million. The G7 agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves.

Cornell's trustees hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the 2024 Chi Phi assault case. A new Special Committee of Cornell's Board of Trustees said Tuesday that Yates, a partner at King & Spalding, will review how the university prevents and responds to sexual assault and misconduct, including campus police, hearings and discipline, coordination with prosecutors, and oversight of fraternities and sororities. Her team will also examine Cornell's response to the October 2024 allegations by Jane Doe against Chi Phi members, including whether it followed its own policies. Yates will report to the committee, and the board said it intends to share the findings with the Cornell community. The state attorney general's separate criminal investigation continues; no criminal charges have been filed.

The 2018 Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods will stay in place after U.S. industries asked for them to continue, the U.S. Trade Representative said. USTR's notice, "Continuation of Actions: China's Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation" (FR Doc. 2026-20510), went on Federal Register public inspection Tuesday and publishes Oct. 7. It comes out of the second four-year review of the tariffs, which began in May. A companion notice (2026-20511) makes conforming changes to product exclusions.

A Nigerian Air Force transport plane crashed in Ondo State, killing all 25 people aboard, the Air Force said. The ATR-42, NAF 931, was on a routine flight from Benin City to Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda on Oct. 5. It carried five crew and 20 passengers. On Tuesday the Air Force confirmed there were no survivors, released the victims' names and ordered an investigation.

Russia told the WHO no plague case has been recorded in Irkutsk and that the dead lab worker's contacts tested negative; about 60% have left quarantine. WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier read Russia's official reply at a Geneva briefing Tuesday: "No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk," and tests of everyone identified as a contact were negative for dangerous pathogens, Reuters reported. Rospotrebnadzor again said testing found no microorganisms linked to the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute technician's work, and a Shelekhov district official said about 60% of those quarantined have been released. Russia's reply did not say whether plague was ruled out in the worker herself, whom officials say died Oct. 2 of pneumonia of unknown cause. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information and that Washington is watching "hour by hour"; the WHO still rates the risk to the general public as low.

Kenya confirmed its first imported Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who traveled from Congo through Uganda and died in Nairobi. Health Minister Aden Duale said Tuesday the patient arrived in Kenya on Saturday and was isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital before dying.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution by firing squad was approved by President Trump; the U.S. military has not executed anyone since 1961. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X that the Army secretary will set the time and place. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that killed 13 people.

A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile Monday evening, starting an engine-room fire, the UK maritime agency UKMTO said. UKMTO cited the ship's captain and said there were no early reports of injuries. It is the third tanker struck in two days, after a crude tanker Saturday and an oil tanker and an LNG tanker Sunday. Iran's Fars news agency said Iran had acted against 13 vessels in the past seven days. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards turned an inbound tanker back on Monday.

A Trump executive order lets off-road dyed diesel be used on highways through Dec. 31 and moves to defer the federal diesel excise tax. The order, "Emergency Tax Relief on Diesel Fuel," was signed Oct. 5. Treasury has five days to decide whether disaster-style relief applies; if it does, federal diesel excise tax payments are deferred for fuel used Oct. 5 through Dec. 31. The IRS must also announce within five days that it will not penalize selling or using dyed diesel on highways in that period. The White House says the deferral carries no interest or penalties and that Europe agreed to release 100 million barrels of refined diesel from its reserves over four months.

The Supreme Court opened its new term by turning away hundreds of appeals, including Second Amendment, COVID vaccine-mandate and "Let's Go Brandon" cases. Monday's order list from the justices' Sept. 28 long conference denied review in United States v. Hembree, leaving in place a 5th Circuit ruling that the federal felon-in-possession gun ban was unconstitutional as applied to a man whose prior felony was meth possession. The Court also denied two challenges to Washington state COVID-19 vaccine mandates (Petersen v. Snohomish Regional Fire and Rescue; Roberts v. Ferguson) and left in place a 6th Circuit ruling letting a Michigan school bar "Let's Go Brandon" sweatshirts. In Mullin v. National TPS Alliance, it sent the Venezuelan and Haitian Temporary Protected Status case back to the 9th Circuit in light of its June ruling in Mullin v. Doe, and it asked the Solicitor General for views in three mortgage-escrow interest cases. The Court heard its first argument of the term, Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, on whether federal law bars state climate-damage suits against oil companies.

Treasury warned foreign banks still doing business with Iran's financial sector that they can be sanctioned at any time, without advance notice. The OFAC alert, dated Oct. 5 under "Operation Economic Outcast," tells banks dealing with sanctioned Iranian banks to end those ties right away and says serving Iranian banks or their branches abroad now carries sanctions risk. OFAC also amended an Iran FAQ on restricting a foreign bank's U.S. correspondent accounts. Earlier steps include cutting Banque Misr UAE's U.S. correspondent access in August and sanctioning Turkey's Golden Global Bank and Russia's VTB Bank in September.

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31% Monday, its highest level since 2002. The benchmark yield rose 3.4 basis points on the day, Dow Jones Market Data reported, extending a selloff that pushed it to a 19-year high in late September. Big tech shares still lifted stocks, and the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on worries about France's debt. U.S. crude for November fell 1.84% to settle at $89.43 a barrel. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgage and other long-term loan rates.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces retook Dhubab and other towns near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from the Houthis, Yemeni officials said. The offensive, called "Yemen Dawn," also took the towns of Bab and Hadeid, according to officials and witnesses. Saudi coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets are supporting the push. A U.S. official and a regional official told AP the United States provided intelligence sharing, targeting and planning help. Government leaders say the goal is to retake Sanaa. The WHO says the fighting has killed at least 959 people.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards forced an inbound tanker to turn back in the Strait of Hormuz, as a third tanker in two days was hit by a projectile. UK Maritime Trade Operations said Monday the IRGC hailed the tanker 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, and told it to turn back or be targeted; the master complied. Separately, UKMTO said another tanker in the strait was struck by an unknown projectile that set its engine room on fire; the crew was fighting the blaze and no casualties or environmental damage were reported. Iran's parliament speaker said the strait stays closed until seven U.S. conditions are met, and President Pezeshkian called talks with Washington meaningless. Pezeshkian on Sunday accepted the resignation of Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad as exports dried up under the U.S. blockade.

The two passengers on the lost Bermuda–Boston air ambulance were named as a Bermuda mother and son; all six aboard are presumed dead. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as a storm approached. A Florida school bus carrying 37 students flipped in a Winter Haven crash Monday, killing a 10th-grade girl and a Jeep occupant. item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, October 5, 2026
item.description:
Brazil's first-round count has Flavio Bolsonaro leading President Lula, short of a majority, with a runoff on Oct. 25. With 100 percent of polling sections counted early Monday, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party had 56,104,503 votes, 47.03 percent of valid votes, and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party had 53,879,538, 45.16 percent, O Globo reported from Superior Electoral Court data. Augusto Cury was third with 2.89 percent. Neither reached the more than 50 percent of valid votes needed to win outright, so the two meet in a runoff on Oct. 25. Abstention was about 21 percent, the highest since 1998.

Russia launched 205 drones at Ukraine overnight; jet-powered drones killed one person and injured eight in Kharkiv, officials said. Ukraine's Air Force said the attack began at 6 p.m. Sunday Kyiv time and included 49 jet-powered Shahed-type drones; air defenses shot down or suppressed 172 by 8 a.m. Monday, with hits at 13 locations. Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said three Banderol jet drones struck near homes in the Industrialnyi district. Separately, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday the U.S. has proposed technical-level three-way talks with Russia by the end of October and that Ukraine responded positively.

A Merit Systems Protection Board rule ending the required 12-factor review of federal workers' discipline penalties takes effect today. The final rule (Federal Register document 2026-18061, published Sept. 3) replaces the mandatory review of all 12 Douglas factors in misconduct appeals with a test of whether an agency's penalty is reasonable under the totality of the circumstances. It applies to appeals filed on or after Oct. 5; pending appeals stay under the old framework. Individual factors can still be raised, and material mitigating evidence must be considered.

The State Department said it is monitoring a suspected fatal pneumonic plague case in Russia's Irkutsk region with the CDC. A State Department spokesperson told RFE/RL on Oct. 4 that the U.S. is aware of reports of a fatal suspected pneumonic plague case and is monitoring with the CDC and other agencies, and urged Russia to share accurate information quickly and openly; an HHS spokesperson confirmed the CDC is working with State. No new U.S. travel restrictions were announced, and there are no direct commercial flights between the two countries. Russia's Rospotrebnadzor says the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute lab technician died of pneumonia of unknown cause, found no work-linked microorganisms in testing, and calls the regional situation stable; about 200 contacts are under observation.

U.S. B-1 bombers used for Iran strikes have left Britain's RAF Fairford and returned home, the Pentagon confirmed. The Pentagon said Sunday that all U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford had re-deployed to their home stations, without saying when they moved or why, and that the bomber force can still strike from the continental United States. The move follows a U.K. counterterrorism investigation near the base: police arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian man in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, and five U.K. nationals arrested Sept. 27 over suspicious vehicles near the base were released on bail.

Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced a military campaign to retake all territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised address Sunday that operations would continue until the country is freed from the Houthis, after de-escalation efforts were exhausted; a military spokesman told the Houthis to lay down their weapons. The Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, in an offensive last month, and AFP, citing Yemeni military sources, reported they cut the road linking Taiz with Aden on Sunday. The same day, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group fired missiles and drones at Aramco sites in Riyadh and Khurais; Saudi Arabia had not commented.

France's high-school protests will close up to 500 schools fully or partly Monday, the education minister said; 24 have been burned or ransacked. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Sunday that lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools where security conditions are not met, about the same number as Friday, with a "partial, progressive return" to classes. He said 24 schools have been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff injured since the movement began. More than 5,000 people, about 85 percent of them minors, have been arrested. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu sent ministers a roadmap Sunday asking that classes resume wherever safety allows and setting a timetable to answer some student demands, including school renovation talks with regional presidents and Parcoursup proposals by the end of October. In the Paris region, more than 160 of 468 public high schools will be closed Monday, regional president Valerie Pecresse said. A 16-year-old was detained Sunday over Friday's assault on a 59-year-old teacher who was doused with gasoline and struck in La Ciotat. Organizers have called for more protests Tuesday.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, as drones hit a Kyiv bridge for a fourth straight day. The ministry said the stepped-up attacks on military, defense-industry and related infrastructure respond to President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's vow in a Reuters interview to hit more Russian oil refineries. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were hurt Sunday when a drone struck the Northern Bridge's roadway, a second straight day of hits there. Zelenskiy said a drone killed one person at a Sumy medical-supplies warehouse and six were hurt at a Dnipro communications site; he said Russia fired more than 1,900 drones, 1,700 glide bombs and 25 missiles over the past week. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made an unannounced visit to Kyiv.

Ethiopian government-allied forces entered Mekelle, the Tigray capital, after TPLF rebels announced they had withdrawn following renewed fighting. The Tigray People's Liberation Front said Saturday its forces had pulled out of Mekelle, which they seized along with its airport last month; a witness said government-allied fighters entered the city Sunday. Residents described looting of the TPLF administration office and regional police headquarters as rebel fighters left. Internet and phone outages have made events hard to verify. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea on Thursday and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats; Eritrea said it was cutting diplomatic ties.

A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged its engine room, UKMTO said. UK Maritime Trade Operations Warning 150-26, issued Oct. 4, 2026, says the master of a tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing engine-room damage. The crew were reported safe and there was no environmental impact reported at the time. Authorities are investigating. Vessels were advised to transit with caution. The report is distinct from earlier UKMTO warnings on Oct. 1–2 tanker hits in and near Hormuz.

The air ambulance search moves to the seabed: the Coast Guard says sonar-equipped craft will scan near the debris field about 20 miles off Nantucket. At a Sunday briefing at Base Boston, the Coast Guard said crews with the New York Air National Guard and Massachusetts authorities have searched about 2,840 square miles for the six people aboard the Gulfstream G100 medical flight from Bermuda to Boston, and are working with Massachusetts authorities to get sonar-equipped vessels over the seafloor. Next of kin are being kept informed. The six — four Canadians and two Bermudians — remain missing.

Trump announced a federal AI task force, the "Super Intelligence Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. In a Truth Social post Sunday, the president said the force will coordinate federal engagement with AI companies, consumers, public-interest and religious groups, and infrastructure providers. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and OPM Director Scott Kupor will also lead it, reporting to Trump and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. It follows last week's White House meeting where OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceXAI signed voluntary safety standards, including internal evaluations, outside audits and board reviews. Trump also named John Coale special presidential envoy for hostage affairs.

A shooting at a block party in Vienna, Georgia, killed two people and injured 35, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said. The GBI said Dooly County deputies were on patrol at the neighborhood party when shots were fired from the 900 block of Pine Street at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday. Two people were found dead in the 600 block of Pine Street, and victims were taken to several regional hospitals. No arrest has been announced; a $5,000 reward has been offered for information.
